title: Reclassify global default set: move project-specific skills out of global
description:
Currently all 78 canonical skills are globally deployed by default. Per the scoping design (docs/scoping-rationale.md), the global set should contain only the TRULY UNIVERSAL skills — everything else becomes project-add-only.

Obvious candidates to move OUT of global (into project-add territory):
- cbm (codebase intelligence — only wanted in code projects)
- shopping-management, ticket-management, ticket-audit, ticket-find, filing-process, etc. (personal/workflow skills not relevant to code work)
- use-railway (deployment context, project-specific)
- Any code-specific skill that shouldn't trigger in non-code sessions

The mechanism ships first (skills-81s) with global-manifest.toml listing everything, so behaviour is unchanged. THIS ticket then curates global-manifest.toml down to the universal core, incrementally — no need to get it perfect in one pass.

Process: for each skill, ask 'would I want this in every session regardless of project?' If no, remove from global-manifest.toml. It remains canonical and available via project add/exclude.

This is governance work, not code — but it's the bulk of making scoping actually useful. Without it, the global set stays bloated and the project-add mechanism has little to add.

# Phase 2 Brief — Global-Default Reclassification (skills-2gs)

**Audience:** executing agent. **Reviewer/consolidator:** the supervisor
(the agent that produced `docs/skills-audit.md`). **Report back at each
checkpoint.**

## Background you must read first

- `docs/skills-audit.md` — the facet framework, the treatment palette
  (esp. Keep-global #1 vs Project-scope #2 vs Library/on-demand #3), and
  the trigger-quality problem (Phase 5 / Cluster G).
- `docs/scoping-rationale.md` — the *why* of global vs project scoping, and
  the resolution rule `resolved = (global_default - exclude) + add`.
- `README.md` — deploy mechanics and the scoping examples.

## The goal

Move skills that don't belong in every session out of `global-manifest.toml`,
so the global default stops being a lowest-common-denominator that triggers
irrelevant skills. Per the scoping rationale: niche skills stay in the repo
(Project-scope or Library/on-demand), available via a project's `add`, but
not shipped to every session by default.

This is **Phase 2 of 5**. It is independent of Phase 1 (note successor) and
Phase 3 (coding-agent architecture). It does **not** retire or rewrite any
skill — it only changes which scope each is deployed at.

## The baseline (verified 2026-07-01)

`global-manifest.toml` currently lists **76 skills** (post Phase-0). Of
those, **12 still drive the dead me-CLI** and are Phase 4 salvage/archive
candidates — they must not stay in global regardless, but their *disposition*
(salvage vs archive) is Phase 4's call, not this phase's. Here they are
neither salvaged nor archived; this phase only **removes them from global**
and leaves them in-repo pending Phase 4.

## Reclassification criteria (the rule)

A skill belongs in global default only if it is **role-universal** — the job
is needed in (nearly) every session regardless of project. Apply these
tests; move out of global if any is true:

1. **Dead mechanism** — drives a system that no longer exists (the me-CLI
   skills). Move out of global; disposition handled in Phase 4.
2. **Domain-niche** — serves a specific domain/language/tool not present in
   most sessions (a language, a business domain, a specialist tool). Belongs
   in Library/on-demand or Project-scope.
3. **Experimental / not-active** — a self-contained experiment worth keeping
   but not currently in use (the go-slice quartet + slice-supervisor).
   Library/on-demand, pending a spin-off decision.
4. **Tangle-pending** — entangled in an unresolved architecture decision
   owned by Phase 3 (the coding-agent cluster). Leave in-repo; this phase
   does not resolve the tangle, but may move clearly-peripheral members out
   of global if unambiguous.

Everything else stays global.

## Proposed triage (checkpoint: report back before editing)

Apply the criteria to the 76-skill baseline. Suggested buckets — **the
reviewer must approve before you edit the manifest.**

### Move OUT of global (dead mechanism — Phase 4 dispositions them later)
- `change-manage`, `feature-build`, `filing-process`, `jot-capture`,
  `location-manage`, `orientate`, `project-manage`, `remind-management`,
  `shopping-management`, `source-management`, `subscription-management`,
  `system-self-care`

  All 12 drive the dead me-CLI. Removing from global stops them
  auto-triggering now; Phase 4 decides salvage-rewrite vs archive. They
  stay in-repo (tracked), just not deployed globally.

### Move OUT of global (domain-niche → Library/on-demand)
- **Languages:** `clojure`, `fsharp`, `nushell`, `ruby` — only relevant when
  working in that language. (Note: all four also have empty descriptions +
  `disable-model-invocation`, so they never auto-trigger anyway — removing
  from global formalises that.)
- **Domain:** `pharmaceutical-definition-creator`, `ruby-code-analysis` —
  specialist, low-frequency.
- **Tools (specialist):** `troubleshoot-codex` (Codex-specific repair),
  `database-migration` (SurrealDB/me-cli-specific — also partly dead-mechanism;
  flag this), `logseq-markdown` (Logseq-specific; vault is moving to
  Obsidian).

### Move OUT of global (experimental → Library/on-demand, pending spin-off)
- `go-slice-implementer`, `go-slice-planner`, `go-slice-reviewer`,
  `slice-retro`, `slice-supervisor` — the go-slice experiment. Per the
  audit: preserve as a unit, not active.

### Leave IN global (role-universal) — but flag for Phase 3
- The coding-agent cluster (`supervisor`, `orchestration`, `discovery-architect`,
  `feature-handoff`, `spike-planning`, `write-design-doc`, the four
  `agent-*` workflow skills, the `*-change-manage`/`*-vcs` skills). Phase 3
  may restructure these, but they're not niche — leave global unless Phase 3
  says otherwise. Exception: **`orchestration` is a self-flagged WIP
  skeleton with a dead dependency** — candidate to move out regardless. Flag
  it; let the reviewer decide.

### Clearly stay IN global
- `br`, `filesearch`, `file-introspection`, `code-and-docs-search`, `cbm`,
  `cheatsheets`, `bin-creator`, `fs-reorg`, `code-review`,
  `root-cause-debugger`, `typst`, `skills-manage`, `tool-eval`, `zcode`,
  `op-env-wrap-tool`, `retro`, `verify`, `update-docs`, `wrap`,
  `documentation-writer`, `mcp-manage`, `work-unit-manage`, `use-railway`.

### Vendored (gitignored — review separately)
- `article-extractor`, `csv-data-summarizer`, `last30days`, `nia`,
  `omnigraph`, `ship-learn-next`, `tapestry`, `total-recall`,
  `youtube-transcript`, `almanac`, `lark-crm`. These are third-party.
  `lark-crm` and `almanac` are clearly live+used; the rest — check whether
  each is actively used or library-only. Report findings; don't assume.

## Deliverables

### D1 — Confirm/amend the triage (checkpoint)

Read each skill's SKILL.md you're unsure about. Amend the buckets above with
evidence. **Report back the final bucketing for approval before editing
anything.** Specifically resolve:
- `database-migration` — is it dead-mechanism (me-cli) or partly live?
- `orchestration` — move out or leave for Phase 3?
- Each vendored skill — actively used or library-only?

### D2 — Edit `global-manifest.toml` (after D1 approved)

Remove the agreed-out skills from the `skills = [...]` array. **Do not
delete any skill directories** — they stay in-repo, just out of global
default. Update the manifest comment if it references a count.

### D3 — Documentation + deploy
- Update `README.md` "What's here" count + any category rows if the
  categorisation implies changes (probably not — categories stay; only
  scoping changes).
- Add a one-line note to `README.md` scoping section clarifying that skills
  not in global-manifest are still in the repo and available via a
  project's `add`, if such a note doesn't already exist (it likely does —
  check).
- Run `./deploy/skills-deploy deploy --dry-run` and report the summary.
  Expect many `remove (would back up + delete)` lines on global targets —
  that's correct, they back up.
- After reviewer approves the dry-run: deploy, commit, report.

## Constraints

- **Report at D1 and before D2-edits and before D3-deploy.** Three
  checkpoints minimum.
- **No skill directories deleted.** This phase changes scoping only.
- **No salvage rewrites.** The 12 me-CLI skills get removed from global but
  their bodies are untouched — Phase 4 rewrites or archives them.
- Match existing manifest formatting (4-space indent, quoted, alphabetical
  within the array).

## Done looks like

`global-manifest.toml` contains only role-universal skills; niche/dead/
experimental skills remain in-repo, available via project `add`; deploy
clean; commit lands with a clear message. The global trigger surface is
noticeably quieter.

## Related

- `docs/skills-audit.md` — Phases 0–5, treatment palette
- `skills-2gs` — this work's ticket
- `docs/phase1-brief.md` — parallel phase (independent)
- `docs/phase3-brief.md` — not yet written (coding-agent architecture)

# Supervisor review — Phase 2 (skills-2gs)

**Reviewer:** supervisor. **Report reviewed:** `log/2026-07-01-phase2-reclassification.md`.
**Verdict: APPROVED with flags.** The mechanics are sound and verified; a
handful of classification judgments are debatable and warrant the user's
call. None block acceptance.

## Mechanics — verified clean

- Commits `58b6835` (manifest) + `2fe2c4c` (beads sync) + `5d7f49a` (report)
  all exist and land cleanly.
- Manifest: header says "39 skills", actual count is 39. Consistent.
- No skill directories deleted — confirmed sample of 8 moved-out skills all
  still present in-repo.
- No me-CLI skills leaked into global (all 13 correctly removed).
- Deploy reported clean; backup-before-removal behaviour holds.

The agent also correctly caught and fixed two errors in my Phase 2 brief:
`lark-crm`/`almanac` are authored (not vendored), and `use-railway` is
vendored (not authored). Good — that's the kind of verify-against-reality
check the brief asked for.

## Classification — the debatable calls

These are judgment calls the user should confirm. The brief's bar was
"role-universal — needed in (nearly) every session." Against that bar:

### Likely correct (stay global)
- `br`, `filesearch`, `file-introspection`, `code-and-docs-search`,
  `code-review`, `root-cause-debugger`, `cheatsheets`, `bin-creator`,
  `fs-reorg`, `skills-manage`, `zcode`, `documentation-writer`,
  `update-docs`, `wrap`, `retro`, `verify`, `mcp-manage`,
  `op-env-wrap-tool`, `spike-planning`, `discovery-architect`,
  `write-design-doc`, `supervisor` — genuinely cross-project.

### Debatable — leaning keep, but flag
- **`lark-crm`** — the CRM for one solo business. High-quality and
  live, but "role-universal"? It's universal *for this user*, which may be
  the right reading. Lean keep; user confirm.
- **`almanac`** — drives the CodeAlmanac CLI. Keep only if almanac wikis
  are part of the daily workflow across projects; if it's one project's
  tool, it's project-scope. User confirm.
- **`cbm`** — "use after code-and-docs-search router has selected it." If
  the router lives globally (it does), keeping the downstream tool global is
  defensible. But it's also exactly the kind of heavy MCP tool a project
  opts into. Lean keep because it's the router's pair.

### Debatable — leaning move OUT
- **`concept-boundary-test` + `concept-layer-synthesis`** — these operate
  on a "Concept Garden," a specific knowledge-management practice. Unless
  concept-garden work happens in most sessions, these are library/on-demand,
  not global. **My recommendation: move both out.** They survived because
  they're authored not vendored, but origin ≠ universality.
- **`typst`** — a typesetting language. Equivalent to the languages that
  were moved out (`ruby`, `clojure`, etc.). Inconsistent to keep `typst`
  global while `ruby` is project-scope. **My recommendation: move out** for
  consistency, unless typst docs are authored in nearly every session.
- **`tool-eval`** — evaluate third-party tools. Useful but infrequent;
  classic library/on-demand. Lean move out, but low stakes either way.
- **`work-unit-manage`** — needs scrutiny. If it's me-CLI coupled (the name
  pattern matches), it may belong with the Phase 4 set. If it's a generic
  work-lifecycle skill, keep. **Recommend the user check its mechanism.**

### Coding-agent cluster (stays global — correct for now)
The 8 coding-agent/VCS skills (`agent-commit-workflow`,
`agent-implementation-strategy`, `agent-task-boundaries`,
`agent-vcs-workflow-with-jj`, `git-change-manage`, `git-vcs`,
`jj-change-manage`, `jj-vcs`) all stayed global. That's the right call
*for this phase* — Phase 3 owns restructuring them. But note: they overlap
heavily (per the audit's Cluster C), so keeping all 8 global means 8
overlapping skills in the trigger surface. Phase 3 should trim this; Phase 2
correctly deferred it.

## Flags for downstream phases

1. **`work-unit-manage` mechanism check** — is it me-coupled? If so it
   belongs in Phase 4, not global. Quick to resolve.
2. **`concept-*` and `typst` consistency** — the language/domain bar was
   applied unevenly. Easy to correct in a follow-up edit if the user agrees.
3. **Phase 3 will reshape the global set further** — the 8 coding-agent
   skills staying global is temporary; expect churn when Phase 3 lands.

## Net assessment

A solid, well-documented execution. The 76→39 cut is aggressive but
defensible, and critically it was *reversible-by-design* (nothing deleted,
all recoverable via project `add`). The corrections to my brief show the
agent verified rather than trusted. The open items are genuine judgment
calls that belong to the user, not defects.

title: Skill quality control: naming convention, linting, and description-driven loading
description: Skill naming is inconsistent and unenforced. Survey of the 81-skill set: object-verb (skills-manage, change-manage, work-unit-manage, location-manage, project-manage, git-change-manage, jj-change-manage - 7 in one family) coexists with verb-object (write-design-doc, update-docs, use-railway), noun-agent (discovery-architect, documentation-writer, go-slice-planner, bin-creator), and bare verbs (plan, verify, wrap, orientate, retro). Near-duplicate concepts exist (documentation-writer AND documentation-writing; four overlapping change-management skills). No convention is documented or enforced. THREE related gaps in priority order. (1) AUTO-LOADING via description quality: a skill only helps if it loads at the right moment; descriptions must be strong enough to trigger reliably (skills-manage should auto-load before ANY skill authoring, not wait to be remembered). A skill that is not loaded is invisible - this is the highest-impact gap. (2) LINTING: enforce naming convention, frontmatter schema, description quality, and duplicate-concept detection as a deploy/reconcile check. Likely existing tools (skillkit is half-present; community skill-linters exist). (3) EVALS: no way to test a skill improves agent behavior or loads in the right contexts. All three are one root problem: skills authored by hand with no quality gate between authoring and deploy. This issue scopes the work, does not solve it now.

title: Warn on deploy when canonical skills are absent from global-manifest.toml
description:
Footgun surfaced while deploying skills-manage: adding a skill to canonical does NOT automatically add it to global-manifest.toml, so it silently won't deploy. Since deploy reads the manifest (not canonical directly) to determine the global set, a new skill is invisible until the manifest is manually edited.

This is inherent to the explicit-manifest design (reclassification ticket skills-2gs relies on the manifest being curated deliberately), but it's a real footgun for rapid skill creation — you author a skill, deploy, and wonder why it's missing.

Fix: deploy should warn when canonical contains skills not present in global-manifest.toml. The warning should:
- Fire at the start of a global deploy (not project deploy — projects use add/exclude)
- List the canonical skills missing from the manifest
- Suggest adding them to global-manifest.toml (or note they're available only via project add, which may be intentional)
- Be a WARNING, not an error — deploy should still proceed (the manifest is authoritative for what's global; missing skills may be deliberately project-add-only)

This pairs with the reclassification effort: once global-manifest is curated down (skills-2gs), MOST canonical skills will legitimately be absent from global and this warning would fire constantly. So the warning should probably distinguish 'recently added and likely forgotten' from 'deliberately not global'. Simplest heuristic: only warn if the skill was added to canonical recently (e.g. mtime within last N days) AND is absent from manifest. Or: make it informational (--strict flag to promote to error). Decide on the shape during implementation.

Related: the manifest header already has a NOTE about this friction (added in the drift-prevention commit).
close_reason: Implemented in commit 819de03. Global deploy warns when canonical has skills absent from global-manifest.toml; --strict promotes to error (exit 1). Project scope exempt. Tested all scenarios.

title: AGENTS.md instruction files are unmanaged — no source of truth, drift risk
description:
Surfaced during skills-management work. The always-loaded instruction files — ~/.agents/AGENTS.md (opencode family) and ~/.codex/AGENTS.md (Codex) — are currently hand-maintained with no source of truth, no version control, and no deploy mechanism. They contain substantial content (tool-selection guidance, Nia workflow, RTK commands, codebase-memory priority order) that lives only on this machine.

This is a parallel problem to the skills drift we just solved: these files are high-leverage (loaded every session, reach every agent before any skill) but completely unmanaged. If this machine died, they'd be gone.

The skills-manage effort needs to add a small note to these files (skills authoring location + pointer to skills-manage skill), which makes the unmanaged-ness acute: we're about to inject canonical-store metadata into files that have no canonical home of their own.

Scope of the real problem (separate effort):
- Where do AGENTS.md files get authored? (A dir in Dotfiles? A new canonical store? Per-harness variants?)
- How do they deploy? (symlink from Dotfiles already does this for some — ~/.config/opencode is symlinked — but ~/.codex/AGENTS.md and ~/.agents/AGENTS.md are plain files)
- How are per-harness differences handled? (Codex AGENTS.md has RTK/codebase-memory content; opencode has tool-selection/Nia — they're not identical)
- Version control?

Out of scope for skills-manage but flagged here so it's tracked. The skills-manage note will be hand-added to AGENTS.md for now, accepting the unmanaged-ness as a known cost.

title: Implement project-scoping: --dest flag + manifest resolution
description:
Extend skills-deploy with two-scope deployment per docs/scoping-rationale.md.

Scope 1 — global (already works, needs the manifest):
- Read repos/skills/global-manifest.toml (list of canonical skill names that ship by default)
- skills-deploy deploy mirrors ONLY that set to ~/.agents/skills + ~/.codex/skills (currently mirrors everything)

Scope 2 — project (new):
- Add --dest <project-dir> flag
- Read <project-dir>/.agents/skills-manifest.toml (add + exclude fields)
- Resolve: (global_default - exclude) + add
- Mirror resolved set into <project-dir>/.agents/skills/ AND <project-dir>/.codex/skills/ if it exists
- Same mirror semantics: remove skills not in resolved set (with backup), skip symlinks/.system

Manifest format documented in docs/scoping-rationale.md.
Start with global-manifest.toml listing ALL current skills (so behaviour is unchanged until the reclassification ticket runs).

Key constraints:
- One manifest per scope, fanned to all harness dirs at that scope (no per-harness manifests)
- Project skills dir cleaned via mirror, not just appended
- No per-skill frontmatter flags (rejected — see rationale doc)

See docs/scoping-rationale.md for the full design and rejected alternatives.

title: br step 5 ('commit .beads/') contradicts harness 'commit only when user asks'
description:
## Problem

`br` SKILL.md "Required Workflow" step 5 (line 55):
> 5. Commit `.beads/` — the JSONL is already current.

…and the `br` cheatsheet:
> Committing `.beads/` is your job.

…are unconditional. They do not reconcile with the harness rule "commit or push only when the user asks" or with the default-branch caveat. An agent following `br` literally will commit `.beads/` (and likely the associated work) on `main` without consent; an agent that notices the conflict freezes.

This is the direct trigger of the `agents-gb8` incident: the br workflow said commit, the harness said don't, no skill reconciled them.

## Fix

Two options (pick at build time):

1. **Soften step 5 to point at the policy.** Reword to: "Commit `.beads/` per the commit policy in `git-vcs` — the JSONL is already current, so no flush step is needed." This keeps the operational fact (no flush needed) while routing the WHEN decision to the canonical policy once skills-commit-when-policy-gap-r8e lands.

2. **Scope step 5 to `.beads/` only.** Make clear that the br workflow authorizes committing the tracker JSONL specifically (a bookkeeping artifact, low-risk), and that committing the *work* itself follows the general commit policy. This matches user mental model: "closing a ticket" naturally includes committing the tracker; "closing a ticket" does not naturally include committing code on main.

Option 2 is probably cleaner — the br skill shouldn't be in the business of authorizing code commits at all. But it must say so explicitly, or agents will read step 5 as blanket license.

## Dependency

Resolve after or alongside skills-commit-when-policy-gap-r8e — the fix references the policy that ticket creates.

comments.author: bear
comments.text:
REFRAME from user (corrects the framing):

Issue tracking is orthogonal to committing code. `br` only mentions commits because it is a flat-file tracker that needs its JSONL saved — that is incidental to br's file-based storage, not a statement about when code commits are authorized. If the tracker were Linear (remote, no local file to commit), br's commit line would vanish entirely and the code-commit policy would not change by one millimetre.

So this ticket's original framing — "br step 5 contradicts the harness" — is wrong. br is not a competing authority on code commits; it's noise that leaked into the conversation because of an implementation detail of the tracker. The real issue lives in the VCS/coordination layer, not in br.

REVISED FIX DIRECTION: br step 5 should be reworded to be unambiguous about its scope — it is about persisting the tracker's own state (a bookkeeping artifact), NOT about authorizing commits of the work being tracked. Something like: "Commit `.beads/` so the tracker state is persisted — this is bookkeeping for the tracker itself, separate from any decision to commit the work." That removes the over-read without br pretending to be a commit authority.

This makes the ticket mostly a wording-clarity fix in br, not a policy contradiction. The policy contradiction is fully owned by skills-commit-when-policy-gap-r8e and the new structural ticket on git-workflow / git-change-manage / coordination-protocol overlapping concerns.

title: coordination-protocol 'certainty cascade' failure-mode overgeneralizes to any irreversible action
description:
## Problem

`coordination-protocol/SKILL.md` transition rule (lines 58-68) defines the "certainty cascade" failure mode. It is precisely scoped to *conceptual reorganizations* — baking a new frame into the tracker/docs/workspace before the user confirms it:

> WHEN the agent produces a re-framing of the work ... → check the frame with the user *before* reorganizing tickets, docs, or plans around it.

That's correct and well-scoped. The problem is the rule's *reception*. Read in isolation alongside the harness rule "commit only when the user asks" and `git-vcs`'s "never push unless explicitly asked," a careful agent generalizes the certainty-cascade lesson to *any* irreversible-seeming action — including a local commit on a feature branch, which is trivially reversible (`git reset`) and is supposed to be part of the work unit.

This is a secondary contributor to the `agents-gb8` freeze: not the primary trigger (that's the missing WHEN policy, skills-commit-when-policy-gap-r8e) but an amplifier. The agent had a vague sense that "pausing to verify is the work" applied more broadly than the rule actually states, which made the freeze feel principled rather than confused.

## Fix

Add a scoping clause to the certainty-cascade rule that names what it does NOT cover. Something like:

> This governs conceptual reorganizations — restructuring the tracker, rewriting plans, renaming the work's frame. It does not govern reversible execution steps that the work unit already authorizes (a local commit on a feature branch, a new file in a scratch dir). Conflating the two produces false caution: the agent freezes on authorized work and calls the freeze diligence.

One sentence. Keeps the rule's precision intact while preventing the generalization that produces the false-caution failure mode.

## Why P2 not P1

The rule itself is correct as written; this is a defensive clarification against misreading. The primary fix is the commit-WHEN policy (skills-commit-when-policy-gap-r8e). But without this clarification, even a correct policy may be over-ridden by an agent reasoning "the certainty cascade says pause."
close_reason: Implemented the requested scope clarification in agent-workflow/coordination-protocol/SKILL.md: certainty-cascade applies to conceptual re-framing and tracker/plan/workspace reorganisation, not as a blanket pause before reversible execution; local VCS authorisation remains owned by work-unit/VCS policy. Verified 2026-08-11.

title: No skill states WHEN a local commit is authorized — only HOW
description:
## Problem

The VCS skills (`git-vcs`, `git-change-manage`, `work-unit-manage`) define how to commit — staging deliberately, atomic boundaries, linear history — but none state **when a local commit is authorized by the work unit itself**. This is the load-bearing gap. An agent that knows how to commit but not when will either (a) commit unprompted and risk the user's "only when I ask" rule, or (b) freeze and dress the freeze up as "leaving it for your review." Both happened this session.

## Concrete incident

Closing `agents-gb8` in the agents repo (work on `main`, three new files + Makefile edit, `make test` green). The `br` skill's step 5 says commit `.beads/`; `skills-manage` lists "forgetting to commit after authoring" as a common mistake; the harness says "commit only when the user asks." With no WHEN policy, the agent held the commit and framed the hold as a courtesy. User caught the tell: "I think you are exposing contradictory advice."

## The three signals in conflict

- **Commit (workflow step):** `br` SKILL.md step 5 — "Commit `.beads/`." `br` cheatsheet — "Committing `.beads/` is your job." `skills-manage` common-mistakes — "Forgetting to commit after authoring."
- **Don't commit (harness):** harness system prompt — "Commit or push only when the user asks." Also "if on the default branch, branch first."
- **Conservative tenor (vcs):** `git-vcs` — "Never fetch, pull, push, or force-push unless explicitly asked." Says nothing about local commits on a feature branch, but the ask-first tenor leaks.

## What's missing

A short, canonical policy — ideally one block in `git-vcs` or a new `commit-policy` section in `work-unit-manage` — that names:
1. A local commit on a non-default branch is part of the work unit and needs no separate authorization. The `br` step-5 / `skills-manage` commit-after-authoring rules apply.
2. A commit on `main`/`master` requires branching first (aligns with the harness rule) OR explicit user consent to commit on main.
3. Push, force-push, and remote operations always require explicit ask (already in `git-vcs`; just needs to be clearly demarcated from local commit).

Without this, every agent hits the same fork and resolves it inconsistently.

## Proposed location

`git-vcs/SKILL.md` is the natural home — it's the shared git adapter and the first skill loaded for any git operation. Add a "When to commit" subsection between Core Rules and Safe Inspection. Cross-reference from `br` step 5 and `work-unit-manage` End phase so the three pulling skills point at the single source.

## Repro

Any task that (a) runs in a git repo, (b) closes a br ticket, (c) touches code on the default branch. Watch the agent's closing line. If it invents a reason to hold the commit ("left for your review", "uncommitted to allow inspection"), that's this gap surfacing.

comments.author: bear
comments.text:
ADDITIONAL CONTEXT from user (sharpens the fix):

Two clarifications that should shape the canonical policy:

1. The harness rule "commit or push only when the user asks" is the DEFAULT policy and clearly needs overriding under certain circumstances. The fix is not to weaken it or work around it — it is to name, explicitly and in one place, the circumstances under which a local commit is part of the work unit and needs no separate authorization. The harness stays as the floor; the policy names the legitimate exceptions.

2. The "forgetting to commit after authoring" line in skills-manage (common-mistakes list) is scoped to authoring within the skills repo specifically — it is not a general commit-authorisation rule. But because it reads as general, it muddies the water. Two options: (a) delete the line entirely on the grounds that a clear commit policy makes "forgetting" impossible if the process is followed; (b) keep it but scope it explicitly to skills-repo authoring. User leans toward (a) — if the commit workflow is clear enough, the "forgetting to commit" mistake shouldn't exist as a category at all.

Proposed rule: local commits are authorised as reversible boundaries for a scoped work unit; push, merge, deploy and publish remain separate approval gates. Awaiting user adoption/amendment before changing skill policy.

title: Rationalise operational skills around a phase-transition state machine
description:
Problem

The operational skill set has accumulated overlapping workflow policy across coordination-protocol, supervisor, wrap, retro and coding-specific slice skills. Some concepts are ambient posture, some are explicit user-invoked operations, and some are local coding-session mechanics, but trigger descriptions and embedded instructions blur those boundaries. This causes accidental invocation, duplicated policy and inconsistent interaction patterns.

Evidence and motivating case

A Chemify phase comparison was accepted by review, yet a candid reflection surfaced several consequential decisions that had to be resolved before Stage 4. The accepted output was complete, but the next phase was not ready. A one-question-at-a-time decision dialogue then worked unusually well: each question supplied the bigger picture, a concrete illustration, options, trade-offs, a recommendation and an explicit human choice. Existing supervisor guidance instead recommends clustering 2–4 questions. The current retro skill is also implicitly invocable for ordinary words such as retrospective even though its actual purpose is narrow operational kaizen: friction, root cause and durable system improvement.

Architectural hypothesis

Treat phase transition as a soft state-machine gate, distinct from output acceptance:

Executing -> Reviewing -> Accepted(output) -> Transition check
Transition check -> Ready
Transition check -> Reflection required -> Reflecting -> Decisions pending -> Decision dialogue -> Brief rewrite -> Ready

The agent evaluates fuzzy guard conditions; the human decides material frame, scope, policy and trade-off questions. State and evidence should be externalised in artefacts rather than hidden in conversation.

Proposed boundaries

- coordination-protocol owns ambient phase states, transition guards and readiness.
- Explicit commands own operational retro, reflection-prompt generation and decision dialogue.
- supervisor/execution skills consume transition state; they should not each reinvent the protocol.
- wrap remains an end-of-session handoff artefact, not a substitute for transition reflection.
- slice-retro remains a structured coding-session subsystem and is not folded into the generic protocol.
- retro should leave global implicit deployment once its explicit command replacement exists.
- Rich decision records should capture the question, context, options, recommendation, user choice and reasoning, consequences, evidence gaps, revisit condition and exact impact on the next brief.

Questions for deeper design

- Which states and guards belong in the ambient protocol versus optional commands?
- How should soft state be represented across single-agent, multi-agent and ticket-driven work?
- When is reflection required, merely useful or unnecessary?
- Should generate-reflection-prompt be domain-neutral with selectable lenses?
- How should decision dialogue resume, revise prior decisions and handle stakeholder evidence arriving later?
- Which duplicated or contradictory policies in operational skills should be removed or delegated?
- How should commands, skills and agent definitions reference one canonical policy without becoming tightly coupled?
- What tests demonstrate that the architecture reduces process accretion rather than adding another layer?

Initial bounded slice

Implement the three explicit commands, remove retro from the global skill manifest, and add the transition gate to coordination-protocol. Keep this epic open for the broader rationalisation and migration.

The agents task must coordinate with this epic rather than define a competing lifecycle.

comments.author: codex
comments.text:
Stage 4 recovery supplied a second, more consequential body of evidence.

Tracker boundary correction
- br and any other tracker integration must be adapters only. Neither a tracker skill nor its cheatsheet should own a ready -> claim -> execute -> close lifecycle; the operational architecture must work with a different tracker.
- Current canonical tools/br/SKILL.md still contains a Required Workflow ending in close. In Stage 4, this sat in tension with review and human-adjudication gates and helped make executor closure appear normal.

Observed failure
- The current user experience is an ad hoc relay between independent Codex threads because context expires. The user manually obtains a handoff and starts the next thread. This is the failure state, not the target architecture.
- A Stage 4 executor produced a strong report but collapsed pre-test reviewers, fresh reasoners, verification and Phase C adjudication into its own narrative; selected Retain despite candidate/supervisor authority; and closed the ticket.
- After interruption, plausible summaries were treated as substitutes for missing durable receipts. Reopening and fresh completion review found the derivative strong but the experiment chronology independently unauditable.

Target hypothesis: artifact-centric orchestration
- Typed information objects form a blackboard: Brief, WorkItem, Artifact, Report, VerificationReceipt, Review, DecisionRequest, Decision, Reflection, Transition.
- A small durable workflow/state-machine kernel owns legal transitions, required receipts, guard evaluation and publication or assignment of eligible work.
- A persistent supervisory control plane orchestrates disposable agents. The user does not carry batons between peer threads.
- Material authority, policy and trade-off guards generate human DecisionRequests.
- Tracker state mirrors the lifecycle but is not its authority.
- Prefer derived state: without a standalone Review object, the phase cannot be reviewed regardless of a report or tracker claim.

Required invariants
1. A report may summarise receipts but cannot substitute for them.
2. Missing receipt means the transition did not occur, especially after interruption.
3. Executors cannot independently verify, adjudicate human authority or close phases.
4. The controller automatically creates verification, review, reflection and next-brief work when guards enable it.
5. Fuzzy guards may be agent-evaluated with rationale; consequential decisions remain human.
6. The user receives decisions, not handoff-management work.

Candidate lifecycle kernel
shaping -> ready-to-execute -> executing -> verification-required -> review-required -> decision-required -> closure-authorised -> closed -> transition-check -> ready-next, with rework/reject branches.

Role ownership
- Executor: Report and completion-evidence manifest.
- Verifier: independently rerun mechanics and issue VerificationReceipt.
- Reviewer: Review against accepted brief.
- Supervisor/controller: publish eligible work and integrate receipts; ideally runtime responsibility rather than a context-heavy persona.
- Human: Decision at material gates.
- Reflection/transition worker: evaluate next-phase guards and produce DecisionRequests or brief updates.

Vertical-slice evidence
chemify-drq.4 was reopened, given a supervisor-owned review brief, reviewed by a fresh bounded agent, and advanced to candidate adjudication. The independent review accepted the content conditionally but classified the executor's clean-room experiment as unproven because actor, context, order and revision receipts were absent.

Design question remains open
Compare a pure blackboard, a durable workflow model and the hybrid. Avoid improving the relay model or redesigning all operational skills before using this fixture to decide where authoritative state and eligibility live.

The Chemify project decision/template/workflow now distinguish executor Report, VerificationReceipt, Review, controlled-access/fresh-recipient receipts and human Decision; reports cannot manufacture independence, chronology or authority. Missing receipt means no transition. This is an accepted requirement for the architecture, not a selection of blackboard, workflow engine or hybrid implementation.

title: br: document the ID naming convention — prefix + code only, no --slug
description:
## Problem

The br skill and cheatsheet do not state the ticket ID naming convention. The tool's \`br create --help\` advertises \`--slug\` as a first-class flag ("keeps the configured prefix and the uniquifying hash suffix"), so agents discovering the tool via --help reach for \`--slug\` and produce long descriptive IDs like \`skills-vcs-workflow-concerns-overlap-k5c\`.

The house convention, visible in the existing ticket set, is prefix + auto-code only:

  skills-8cj, skills-2lm, skills-2gs, skills-kn9, skills-4by, skills-urd  ✓ clean
  skills-vcs-workflow-concerns-overlap-k5c  ✗ slug + code (created this session)

## Decision (settled with user)

IDs are **prefix + auto-code only** (\`skills-8cj\`). Do not pass \`--slug\`.

Rationale: the title already carries the description; the ID just needs to be short, stable, and easy to type into a commit message or cross-reference. The slug-plus-code combined form is the worst of both — it reads as though the slug is the point and the code is the afterthought. Slug-only would be defensible, but the settled lean is code-only.

## Where the convention lives

Two places need a one-line fix:

1. **br SKILL.md Operating Rules** — add a rule naming the convention, in the same form as the existing gotchas. Suggested wording:
   > **IDs are prefix + auto-code.** Do not pass \`--slug\`. The house convention is \`skills-8cj\`, not \`skills-vcs-workflow-concerns-overlap-k5c\`. The title carries the description; the ID stays short and typeable.

2. **br cheatsheet** — either omit \`--slug\` from the flags table, or keep it and mark it "not recommended; house convention is prefix + code only." The create example already uses the bare form (\`br create --actor "$ACTOR" "Title" -p 1 -t task\`), so the examples are correct; only the flags table surfaces the flag without guidance.

The tool's \`br create --help\` text we cannot change — but the skill overrides it, the same way \`skills-manage\` overrides \`skill-creator\`'s location guidance.

## Existing slug-named tickets

Five tickets created this session carry slugs and cannot be renamed (br has no rename capability):

  skills-vcs-workflow-concerns-overlap-k5c
  skills-br-step5-harness-unreconciled-5p1
  skills-commit-when-policy-gap-r8e
  skills-certainty-cascade-overgeneralizes-3xg
  skills-supervisor-references-dir-missing-wr1

Leave as-is — their content and dependency links are intact; migrating would lose comments. The convention fix is forward-looking.

## Related

Two pre-existing slug-named tickets (\`skills-skills-enforcement-scope-xg0\`, \`skills-skills-audit-skill-34c\)) were also agent-created. Confirms the drift is systemic, not a one-off — the silence in the skill is the cause.

**Background:** Phase 1 installed `obsidian-hybrid-search` as the semantic +
fulltext + graph search backend for the `tools/kb` skill. It is currently
**non-functional** — zero indexed, semantic search disabled. The supervisor
diagnosed the root causes during Phase 1 review but bounded further work here
rather than rabbit-hole. This ticket picks up from a known, diagnosed state.

## Current state (verified 2026-07-01)

- `obsidian-hybrid-search` v0.13.16 installed at
  `/Users/bear/.local/share/mise/installs/node/lts/bin/obsidian-hybrid-search`.
- DB exists at `~/Me/kb/.obsidian-hybrid-search.db` (with `-shm`, `-wal`).
- `status` reports: `indexed: 0, chunks: 0, last_indexed: null`.
- **Root cause 1 — embedder unavailable:** the tool wants

  installed with `--no-optional` originally. Attempts to install transformers
  failed: a transitive dep (`sharp`) fails native build; `--ignore-scripts`
  install added packages but node can't resolve them from the hybrid-search

# Skill: facet-based skill-set auditing

Create a skill that captures the improved (second) approach to auditing a
skill set, as demonstrated in `docs/skills-audit.md`.

## Why

The first audit attempt grouped skills into semantic clusters ("me-cli
cluster", "corruption cluster", "thin stubs"). That mixed two different
axes — *what a skill is* (role) and *what's wrong with it* (treatment
needed) — and produced bad triage: it would have discarded durable
role-frameworks (e.g. `orientate`'s drift detection, `feature-build`'s
reflection cycle) just because their backend died.

The second approach separates the axes into orthogonal **facets**, derives
treatment from the combination, and distinguishes eight end-states
(keep-global / project-scope / library / fix / salvage-rewrite / archive /
spin-off / delete) instead of collapsing to "keep or retire." It also
sequences work into dependency-ordered phases, with the systemic
trigger-quality pass last (because retrofitting triggers onto a churning
set is wasted effort).

The improvement is real and generalisable beyond this one audit. Capture it
as a reusable skill.

## What the skill should encode

- **The five facets** — Role, Mechanism, Craft, Differentiation, Trigger
  reach — and the instruction to locate each skill on each independently.
- **Role ≠ mechanism** — the load-bearing principle. A dead mechanism does
  not imply a dead role. Always probe for salvageable detail before
  archiving.
- **The treatment palette** — eight end-states with facet signatures that
  select each. Never underspecify "retire."
- **Phase sequencing** — dependency-ordered; trigger-quality work is last,
  not first.
- **Probe the dead-mechanism set through the salvage lens** as an explicit
  step, with a table (role / mechanism / durable detail / treatment).
- **Bound hard sub-problems into their own tickets** rather than forcing
  premature resolution (the coding-agent architecture pattern).

## Source material

- `docs/skills-audit.md` — the worked example this skill should distil.
- The conversation that produced it (session producing commit following
  `7cd33c1`) — the first-pass clusters vs the second-pass facets.

## Open

- Skill name, category, and whether it's global or library/on-demand.
  (Likely `tools/` or a new `audit/` category; library/on-demand — auditing
  is real but infrequent.)
- Whether to include the full treatment-palette table verbatim or
  reference it from `docs/skills-audit.md`.

comments.text:
# Phase 3 Brief — Knowledge-work orchestration + coding-agent architecture

**Audience:** executing agent. **Reviewer/consolidator:** supervisor.
**Report back at each checkpoint.** This is the hardest phase. It is
foundational: the decisions here shape how all structured work is done,
not just coding.

## Read first

- `docs/skills-audit.md` — facet framework; the coding-agent cluster (C)
  and orchestration trio (B) analysis.
- `docs/phase1-brief.md`, `docs/phase2-brief.md` — the brief/report/review
  cycle that this phase generalises. The artifacts produced there are the
  worked examples of the protocol.
- `tools/br/SKILL.md` — report-placement convention (reports of work belong
  on tickets; standalone docs for reports about work).

## The load-bearing principle: do not assume the work is coding

Most agent-skill work tacitly assumes coding. Terms like "slice,"
"implement," "review," "commit," "verify" carry coding assumptions. **This
phase must not build the foundational orchestration layer on those terms.**
Non-coding structured knowledge work — audits, research synthesis,
planning, documentation, analysis — is equally in scope, and a foundation
baked on coding assumptions will be subtly wrong for it.

The skills-audit session that produced this brief is itself the example: it
was high-value structured knowledge work with no code involved, and it
would have been poorly served by a slice/execute/review framing. The
artifacts (brief, report, review) carried the structure that "tests" and
"build gates" carry in coding.

**Consequence:** separate the *common substrate* (the orchestration
protocol — postures, transitions, artifact conventions, rules) from the
*activity-specific layer* (how you execute a coding slice vs an audit vs a
research synthesis). The substrate is activity-type-agnostic; the execution
content plugs in per type.

## The posture model

Two "supervisor" postures were conflated in the existing skills. Separate
them:

### The entry posture (unnamed in the current set — the real gap)

The user arrives *without* a clear directive — they have a problem, an
unease, a goal — and the agent works **upward**: shapes the ask, grasps the
deeper issue, surfaces what isn't being covered yet, and lands on
scope/outcome/acceptance criteria. This is the posture of a coach, project
manager, and architect combined. It is an intelligent conversational
posture, not a management one.

This is the highest-value gap in the skill set. It is what the
skills-audit session opened with ("I need to do a proper audit… what do you
suggest?") and it was improvised. Parts of it live in `orientate` and
`discovery-architect`, but neither owns it. **Phase 3 must name and capture
this posture.**

Open naming question: "lead" / "orchestrator" / "coach" / other. Do not
bake a name in prematurely; it often becomes obvious during drafting.

### The manage-down posture (`slice-supervisor` is the specialised instance)

Process already determined, work already decomposed, orchestrating
executors against a known shape. Much less vagueness — this is real
supervision. `slice-supervisor` is a *coding-specific, multi-agent*
instance of this. The general posture is prescriptive management.

"Supervisor" fits this posture. Keep it here; do not let it bleed upward.

### The shared spine

Both postures sit above a common pipeline: **clarify → research →
architect → plan → execute → review → consolidate.** Each stage has an
artifact (ask/brief, findings, design, plan, deliverable, review,
writeback). The postures differ in *where they engage* — the entry posture
owns the front of the pipeline (clarify through architect, maybe plan); the
manage-down posture owns the back (plan through consolidate). Same agent
may move between postures; the transition is the conscious decision.

## Activity types — the pluggable layer

The execution stage differs by activity type. Do not assume coding.

| Activity type | Examples | Structure available | Key artifacts |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Coding** | feature, refactor, bugfix, migration | High: slices, tests, review checklists, build/verify gates, VCS conventions | plan, implementation, review, commit |
| **Structured inquiry** | audit, research synthesis, landscape assessment | Lower: process supplied deliberately; artifacts carry the weight | brief, findings, synthesis, report |
| **Planning / design** | architecture, RFC, roadmap | Medium: design frameworks (Diataxis for docs, etc.) | design doc, decision record |
| **Maintenance / triage** | cleanup, reclassification, retirement | Low–medium: checklists, rules | triage table, actions |

The orchestration substrate must work for all four. The execution
*content* (how to slice code, how to structure an audit) is the pluggable
per-type layer.

**"Slice" is a coding concept.** It may be effective in coding contexts and
meaningless elsewhere. Do not put it in the foundational layer. If a
foundational concept is needed for "a bounded unit of execution," use a
neutral term (the audit used "phase"; a plan might call it a "step" or
"workstream") and let coding layer "slice" on top.

## Artifact-driven workflow

The session's brief → report → review cycle worked. Generalise it.

**Principle:** structure the data given to each agent and expected from
each agent, so input/process/output is clear and controllable.

**Light schemas, not heavy ones.** Each artifact *type* has a small
required-elements list and is otherwise freeform:

| Artifact | Required elements | Owner |
|---|---|---|
| **Brief** | scope, checkpoints, done-criteria, what's out of scope | entry/manage-down posture |
| **Report** | what-was-done, evidence, what's-next, deviations | executor |
| **Review** | verdict, defects (with severity), gates passed/failed | reviewer |
| **Plan** | outcome, decomposition, verification approach | planner |

break when work doesn't fit. A convention documented in the orchestration
skill, not enforced by tooling.

## Rules over procedures

Models are improving; procedural directives age badly. Encode the
small-friction decisions (when to log/report/retro/suggest, when to
delegate, when to bound) as **business rules** ("WHEN a stable unit
completes, a progress note exists"), not procedures ("step 7: write a
note").

**Critical caveat:** rules fail silently when incomplete. A procedure that's
wrong produces wrong output predictably (easy to spot); a rule that
doesn't fire produces *no* output. Therefore rules must explicitly cover
**failure modes**, not just the happy path. Source these from real
incidents:

- *When the agent catches itself implementing instead of bounding* → stop,
  write a ticket, return to posture. (The transformers incident during
  Phase 1 is the worked example — the supervisor descended into
  native-dependency debugging instead of bounding a ticket.)
- *When a checkpoint is skipped* → the next stage refuses to proceed
  without the prior artifact.
- *When scope creeps during execution* → executor reports the creep as a
  deviation, does not absorb it silently.

The user uses both git and jj. The "when git, when jj; can tooling separate

Name and capture the managing-up posture. This is the highest-value gap.

  to the general model. Matches the audit's "preserve as a unit" decision.

D4 did exactly what the brief asked. No defects.

## The substantive finding — the skills don't enforce themselves

This is the more important part of the review, and it's about the family
Phase 3 just built, not about D4 specifically.

During D3, the executor committed work without filing the report the
protocol requires (coordination-protocol: "executor produces a report";
execution-spine: "progress notes are not optional"). The reviewer (me)
then accepted a commit SHA relayed in chat as if it were a report, and
wrote the review without noticing the report was missing. Two agents —
the one that wrote the "no artifact, no advance" rule and the one
reviewing the rule — both violated it within minutes of writing it.

**The rule was correct. It didn't fire.** Nothing made it fire. This is
empirical evidence that documented rules in skill prose do not
self-enforce, not even on the agents who just wrote them, not even for
the length of one review cycle. The "no artifact, no advance" gate is
written down; no one operated it.

**Implication for the skill family:** the skills we've built are sound as
*policy* (they define the states, postures, gates, artifacts correctly),
but they are not *enforcement*. The coordination-protocol's gate needs an
honest companion line: *this rule requires a deterministic enforcer — a
reviewer agent's discretion is not sufficient, as the D3 round
demonstrated.* That's not undermining the skill; it's scoping it
truthfully. Without it, the skills imply that writing the rule down is
the work, when the evidence shows it's the smaller half.

**What enforces it is out of scope for the skills themselves.** This is
the gap that the Zenflow/theodosia/open-engine cluster exists to fill,
and it's now backed by an observed, repeated failure (the human-as-queue
during D1–D3, and now the unenforced gate during D3). The policy without
the engine is advice that gets ignored under load. The Zenflow evaluation
(`system-zenflow-eval-05k`) is no longer "does this tool help?" — it's
"which tool provides the specific enforcement primitive we've proven we
need: refuse-advance-until-artifact-exists, wake-reviewer-when-executor-
writes, block-merge-until-review-verdict?"

**Carry-forward:** in the next pass on coordination-protocol and
execution-spine (whether during the Zenflow eval or a follow-up), add the
honest scoping line and make the D3 incident a named worked example, the
same way the transformers descent is. The skills should teach the next
agent what they can and cannot do — and one thing they cannot do is
enforce themselves.

require enforcement beyond prose.

**Recommend closing this ticket** and opening the follow-ups:

title: Bound the overlapping VCS/workflow skills: git-vcs, git-change-manage, work-unit-manage, coordination-protocol have no clean separation
description:
## Problem

The git-workflow / work-unit / coordination layer has overlapping concerns with no clean ownership boundaries. Four skills touch "when and how work becomes a commit" and none of them owns the WHEN:

- `git-vcs` (vcs/) — the git command adapter. HOW to commit. No WHEN.
- `git-change-manage` (vcs/) — work-unit lifecycle in git. HOW to shape a branch/commit. No WHEN.
- `work-unit-manage` (vcs/) — abstract work-unit lifecycle above any VCS. No WHEN.
- `coordination-protocol` (agent-workflow/) — the posture/pipeline/spine layer. Touches commits only via the activity-types table ("Coding: plan, implementation, review, commit") and the certainty-cascade rule.

None of these states when a local commit is authorised by the work unit itself. That gap is tracked separately in skills-commit-when-policy-gap-r8e. THIS ticket is about the structural mess that produced the gap: the concerns overlap and no skill clearly owns which slice.

## User context (verbatim, lightly edited)

> "I'm not a professional software developer and I feel like I'm making more heavy weather of this than a software developer would, where each particular piece of work perhaps has a ticket, and the ticket is claimed and executed, probably in a separate branch or separate worktree, which is something that I don't use. But I feel like I should, and then at the end of it, it sits there — does it? Or is it committed on the branch or worktree and then it's reviewed and then it's merged. Like this stuff is stuff that I just don't understand.
>
> But it feels like the approach should be the same, and I've complicated things for myself by using Git and Jujutsu, so I've got two different systems. And they have two different workflow approaches. Let's forget about Jujutsu for the moment. But there is something here about Git workflow and what this coordination protocol is. This is the stuff that needs to be clearly bounded as separate concerns, each of which have an appropriate skill or cheat sheet or whatever. So there's no overlapping."

## What needs answering (the user's genuine questions)

1. What is the standard shape of a unit of work in git? (ticket claimed → branch/worktree → execute → commit → review → merge?)
2. Does the work sit committed on the branch and get reviewed, or sit uncommitted and get reviewed first?
3. Where does the coordination-protocol layer stop and the git-workflow layer start? They currently overlap.
4. How should this be the same across git and jj (deferred, but the structure should anticipate it)?

These are conceptual questions about workflow shape that a professional git user takes for granted. The skill layer should make them as obvious to a non-professional as they are to a professional. Right now the skills assume the reader already knows the shape and just need command syntax.

## Proposed direction (for build time)

Carve the concerns into non-overlapping slices, each with a clear owner:

- **CONCERN A: git mechanics.** Owned by `git-vcs`. Commands, semantics, safe/unsafe operations. Unchanged.
- **CONCERN B: work-unit shape in git.** Owned by `git-change-manage`. The lifecycle: branch-per-unit, what goes in a commit, when a unit is "done." This is where the WHEN-to-commit policy lives (or is cross-referenced from git-vcs). Adds the standard shape the user is missing: claim → branch → execute → commit → (review) → merge.
- **CONCERN C: abstract lifecycle.** Owned by `work-unit-manage`. Backend-agnostic. Stays above git specifics.
- **CONCERN D: posture / orchestration.** Owned by `coordination-protocol`. Stays out of git mechanics entirely — owns who decides work is ready, not how it's committed.

The certainty-cascade rule in coordination-protocol gets a scoping clause (skills-certainty-cascade-overgeneralizes-3xg) so it stops leaking into git-commit decisions.

## Relationship to the other tickets

- skills-commit-when-policy-gap-r8e — the specific policy fix. This ticket is the structural frame that explains WHY the policy had nowhere to live.
- skills-br-step5-harness-unreconciled-5p1 — br noise, mostly resolved by reframing (see comment). Independent of this structural work.
- skills-certainty-cascade-overgeneralizes-3xg — one symptom of the overlap (coordination-protocol leaking into git decisions).

This is the umbrella. The others are symptoms.

title: Inventory and reconcile all skill stores
description:
## Brief

Create and implement a trustworthy inventory and reconciliation model for the
skills ecosystem. The canonical repository currently contains authored and
vendored skills; the global manifest deploys only a subset to `.agents` and
`.codex`; pi largely points at `.agents`; omp has six managed skills outside
the canonical store; and opencode has a separate local skills directory.

## Required work

- identify every discovered store and its owner;
- compare content, not only skill names;
- classify the six omp skills and the opencode skills as canonical candidates,
  project-local material, vendor material, or intentionally unmanaged;
- decide whether the deploy tool should grow a content-drift/reconciliation
  check and what it should deliberately not manage;
- update the repository documentation and manifests so the model is legible.

## Acceptance criteria

1. The inventory names all stores, their paths, ownership, and synchronisation
   direction.
2. Canonical-versus-target content drift is reported deterministically.
3. Every omp/opencode skill has a recorded disposition; no skill is silently
   lost or promoted to global scope.
4. README, manifest comments, and audit notes agree with the measured counts.
5. Verification commands are documented and run without mutating the targets
   until the release step is approved.

## Constraints

- Do not delete local skills.
- Do not deploy or push as part of this ticket.
- Preserve the current uncommitted `code-and-docs-search` draft for separate
  review rather than treating it as approved source.

title: Add targeted skills deployment mode
description:
# Problem

`skills-deploy deploy --dest <project>` is an all-or-nothing mirror. When a project target has unrelated content drift, a safe update to one canonical skill cannot be deployed without also replacing or removing unrelated target changes.

# Outcome

Add a deliberate, documented single-skill deployment mode (for example `skills-deploy deploy --dest <project> --only <skill>`), which:

- resolves the selected skill against the canonical/project manifest;
- previews the exact copied or removed paths with `--dry-run`;
- changes only that skill directory in each selected target;
- preserves all unrelated target drift; and
- fails clearly if the named skill is not in the resolved set or is ambiguous.

# Acceptance criteria

- A project target can receive one updated canonical skill without mirroring other skill directories.
- Dry-run and real-run behaviour are documented and covered by automated tests or a reproducible harness.
- Existing whole-scope deployment behaviour remains unchanged.
- The command's failure cases are explicit and non-destructive.

# Context

This is needed to deploy the corrected Alan Puzzle `ticket` skill while its `.agents` and `.codex` targets have unrelated drift. It is a deployment-tool capability, not a reason to bulk reconcile a project during a workflow correction.
